candidateRows: Neither causal determination nor indeterminacy permits a person to be the ultimate author or controller of an action.
This causal dilemma supplies the skeptic's foundational argument against ultimate control and applies directly to bodily and mental actions.
After acknowledging the ordinary experience of choosing, Alex analyzes actions through the alternatives of determination and randomness to deny ultimate authorship.
Abstract paradoxes cannot overturn perceptually evident facts, so inquiry into free will must begin from observation and introspection.
The argument establishes Craig's epistemic basis for treating experienced mental agency as evidence despite abstract arguments alleging impossibility.
Alex's abstract determined-or-random argument against experienced control
Craig uses the surprise-quiz puzzle and Zeno's paradox to argue that mental constructions must remain subordinate to perceptual reality.
Causation does not entail necessitation by prior events, and conflating those concepts prejudges the dispute about free agency.
The distinction attacks a key premise of the skeptic's causal dilemma and creates conceptual room for caused but non-necessitated choice.
Alex's claim that every caused event belongs to a determining causal chain
Craig argues that Alex's formulation packages together the distinct claims that events have causes and that prior events necessitate them.
People can introspectively observe themselves regulating mental effort and choosing whether to activate reason, which is the relevant volitional capacity.
This passage supplies the defender's principal positive case that a directly observable capacity for mental focus constitutes free will.
Alex's denial that a decision to focus or deliberate can be under personal control
Craig compares introspection with ordinary perception and argues that awareness of regulating mental effort reveals a choice to engage reason or drift.
Reason and free will are two aspects of one faculty: the ability to think and the capacity to activate that thinking.
The passage defines the precise volitional capacity defended by the pro side and links its existence constitutively to rational agency.
Alex's treatment of reasoning activity as another determined or random mental event
Craig distinguishes rational and emotional functions, then identifies free will with the activation dimension of the human rational faculty.
A person can step back from competing desires, consider broader values, and originate a choice that is caused by the agent without being necessitated by prior factors.
This argument answers both desire determinism and the causal regress by presenting reflective agency as a primary, non-random cause of action.
Alex's contention that motives must be determined by prior causes or occur randomly
Craig says reason can widen the frame beyond whichever desire is strongest and attributes the resulting non-necessitated choice to the acting person.
The felt immediacy of an experience cannot establish its interpretation, because introspection can present illusory forces or agencies as real.
The response undermines the defender's main evidential route from an apparent experience of volition to the reality of free control.
Craig's claim that introspective awareness of mental effort is epistemically self-evident
Alex accepts that abstract reasoning can sometimes mislead but uses the experience of centrifugal force to show that compelling experiences can also mislead.
Attention to deliberation shows thoughts, options, and rational conclusions presenting themselves rather than being proactively selected by a chooser.
This passage directly contests the claimed volitional capacity by arguing that neither deliberative content nor rational conviction is chosen.
Craig's city example and claim that people choose to activate and proceed by reason
Alex revisits the city exercise, argues that alternatives simply arise in consciousness, and maintains that logical conclusions compel rather than await choice.
Agent causation does not end the explanatory regress, because conscious actions follow unchosen desires and the strongest operative desire governs behavior.
The move answers the defender's primary-cause proposal and supplies an alternative mechanism explaining actions without free control.
Craig's claim that the person is a primary cause capable of choosing among desires
Alex asks what caused the agent to cause an action, then argues through drinking and gym examples that action tracks desires whose comparative strength is not chosen.
Even granting a free choice to activate reason would not secure control, because the agent cannot choose what reasoning ultimately makes convincing.
This concessionary argument targets the exact capacity defended by Craig and contends that it cannot deliver control over rational judgment or action.
Craig's definition of free will as the capacity to activate the rational faculty
Alex argues that conviction occurs rather than being selected, then grants activation of reason for argument's sake and denies that it yields mastery over reason's results.
Free will selects the method of conscious engagement rather than subconscious content, allowing reason to alter which desire ultimately governs action.
This defines the precise volitional capacity defended by the pro side and explains how choosing to think can change action without choosing thoughts or desires directly.
O'Connor's claim that neither arising desires nor the activation and conclusions of reason are ultimately under personal control.

After O'Connor argues that attention, desires, and rational conclusions are uncontrolled, Biddle distinguishes chosen cognitive method from unchosen mental content and illustrates its practical effect.
Arguing rationally against free will performatively relies on choosing to activate reason and therefore reaffirms the volitional capacity being denied.
The move supplies a direct self-referential objection to the skeptic's position, alleging that rational advocacy itself presupposes voluntary mental activation.
O'Connor's dichotomy that action occurs only from desire or compulsion and his contention that reason does not establish free will.
Biddle argues that excluding reason reduces argument to emotion, yet O'Connor visibly offers rational arguments, which Biddle treats as an exercise of voluntarily activated awareness.
A free choice is caused by the choosing human agent as an entity, without being random or necessitated by an antecedent event.
This is the pro side's principal causal model for reconciling undetermined choice with causality and answering the skeptic's determined-or-random dilemma.
O'Connor's demand for what causes the decision to activate reason and his contention that an uncaused decision would be random.
Biddle rejects event causation as exhaustive, argues that actions are actions of entities according to their identities, and identifies the person as the non-necessitated cause of choice.
Reason psychologically compels belief when an argument convinces, so reasoning belongs with compelled rather than wanted action and does not presuppose free will.
The move directly contests the proposed volitional faculty by treating rational conviction as an involuntary counterexample and rebuts the performative self-refutation argument.
Biddle's assertion that O'Connor must voluntarily activate reason to argue and therefore uses free will while denying its existence.
O'Connor distinguishes being compelled by a convincing inference from merely wanting to reason, maintaining that conclusions take hold outside the believer's control.
Deliberation changes conduct only by changing which desire is strongest, while both the considerations that occur and the choice to attend to them remain uncontrolled.
This appropriates the defender's leading practical example and redescribes deliberation within the skeptic's desire-based causal account, denying that it demonstrates control.
Biddle's example claiming that choosing to think about long-range values can transform the stronger desire and thereby direct action.
Using the rave and business scenario, O'Connor argues that new considerations simply arise and reorder desires, with any apparent choice to focus itself caused by a prevailing motive.
Agent causation does not explain control because a mental event either has determining causes beyond the agent's ultimate control or occurs causelessly and randomly.
The move restates the skeptic's fundamental exhaustive dilemma against agent causation and directly attacks the pro side's proposed alternative causal explanation.
Biddle's entity-causation account according to which the choosing person causes a decision without antecedent events necessitating it.
O'Connor calls agent causation mysterious, presses for the cause of an agent's act, and argues that material mental activity consists of events subject to the caused-or-random dilemma.
Human consciousness is a real nonphysical existent whose rational faculty operates by choice, so a purely material and mechanistic account is incomplete.
The move supplies the pro side's metaphysical basis for treating mind as an entity with causal powers not reducible to mechanically determined neural events.
O'Connor's conditional argument that reducing mind to brain leaves only mental events that are either determined by causes or random.
Biddle rejects materialism as self-contradictory, treats both external existence and consciousness as directly known, and locates choice in the rational operation of a nonphysical mind.
A universal account of causation must include consciousness, and entity causation permits genuinely volitional causation alongside mechanical and other causal forms.
This develops the causal framework required for the defended form of free will and answers the objection that all causation must mechanically necessitate mental events.
O'Connor's claim that every event, including a mental event, must either have determining prior causes or occur randomly without control.
Biddle argues that causality concerns how every entity acts according to its identity, so consciousness cannot be excluded and choosing to activate reason can itself be causal.
Although present emotions are not directly chosen, repeated choices to think shape value judgments and thereby give people long-term control over their emotional dispositions.
The move answers a major skeptical premise about unchosen desires by explaining an indirect but consequential form of diachronic volitional control over values and emotions.
O'Connor's contention that people do not choose their desires and merely act according to whichever desire becomes strongest.
Biddle concedes that immediate feelings are involuntary but argues that chosen patterns of attention and evaluation form values over time and can harmonize emotion with reason.
The observable capacity to evade recognized facts shows that reason does not force acceptance and provides direct introspective evidence of free will.
This directly rebuts the skeptic's claimed counterexample from compulsory rational belief and offers the pro side's strongest epistemic basis for affirming free will.
O'Connor's argument that once reasoning convinces a person, the resulting belief is compelled and cannot freely be rejected.
Biddle concedes that evidence pressures acceptance but says people can suppress known truths; he treats this ability and regulation of awareness as directly observable rather than inferential.
Integrity and regret presuppose a capacity to choose against one's values by varying the activation of one's mind.
The move connects familiar normative phenomena directly to the claimed volitional capacity and supplies a concrete consequence of denying that capacity.
O'Connor's contention that desires and prior causes explain conduct without any independent volitional faculty.
Biddle argues that loyalty to values, failures of integrity, and retrospective regret make sense because people can activate or neglect their awareness.
Evasion and deliberate desire-change remain explicable through higher-order desires rather than an independent power of free choice.
The move directly contests Biddle's principal evidence for volition by offering a desire-based explanation of both avoidance and long-term self-modification.
Biddle's claim that evasion, compartmentalization, and changing one's conduct demonstrate a freely activated rational faculty.
O'Connor says people suppress considerations because of competing motivations and reshape first-order desires only when a higher-order desire motivates that effort.
Regret is compatible with determinism because new information can reveal that an earlier compelled act conflicted with what the person wanted.
The move blocks a stated pro-side inference from regret to alternative possibility by giving regret a coherent deterministic interpretation.
Biddle's argument that regret would be unintelligible unless a person genuinely could have selected a different action.
O'Connor uses an omitted consideration and later-acquired awareness to explain regret without supposing that the past action was freely avoidable at the time.
Libertarian free will requires a genuine ability to act differently in physically identical circumstances, for which no differentiating explanation is available.
The move defines the disputed libertarian capacity and presents the skeptic's core explanatory challenge concerning divergent actions under identical conditions.
O'Connor defines free will counterfactually, constructs two otherwise identical universes with different shoe choices, and asks what could explain the divergence.
Primary free choice concerns the method of activating awareness, not selecting particular content, while content-level decisions follow secondarily from that method.
This distinction specifies the pro side's actual conception of volition and answers the skeptic's identical-world challenge without positing arbitrary content selection.
O'Connor's challenge asking how physically identical circumstances could yield different specific choices such as different shoes.
Biddle says focus determines whether relevant context enters awareness; resulting shoe choices remain desire-involving outcomes rather than the fundamental locus of freedom.
Choosing fuller awareness can reorganize which desire is strongest, so desire-governed action does not render the volitional act of focusing idle.
The move reconciles Biddle's volitional model with the shared premise that action follows strongest desire, preserving a causal role for chosen awareness.
O'Connor's objection that once focus is activated, values and desires still determine every substantive conclusion and action.
Biddle characterizes focus as a narrow but powerful switch that broadens awareness while conceding that values and desires remain central to subsequent decisions.
A choice to focus is caused by the agent without being necessitated, and its reality is directly observable through changes in one's level of awareness.
The move states the pro side's central causal category, distinguishes causation from necessitation, and supplies its principal epistemic basis for volition.
O'Connor's challenge that a focus choice either has a determining factor or lacks an intelligible causal explanation.
Biddle attributes focus to a rational agent whose faculty operates by choice, treats volition as unusual but real, and appeals to observed modulation of awareness.
Complex deliberation remains nonvolitional because considerations influence conviction at each junction rather than being arbitrarily selectable by the reasoner.
The move generalizes the skeptic's account from simple inference to realistic deliberation, addressing a major objection that complex reasoning contains choices.
The audience objection that real reasoning is a messy, extended process involving many apparent choices rather than mechanical deduction.
O'Connor argues that added complexity does not create arbitrary control: information and reasons move the thinker, who discovers rather than chooses what persuades.
Introspective confidence in free will is defeasible when philosophical considerations provide alternative explanations of the apparent experience.
The move directly challenges the pro side's principal epistemic foundation by distinguishing ordinary reliance on experience from indefeasible introspective proof.
The audience challenge that correcting perceptual errors itself depends on valid sensory evidence and therefore cannot discredit direct experience generally.
O'Connor accepts ordinary perceptual trust but argues that experience alone cannot settle a philosophical dispute once supported reasons make that experience open to doubt.
The alternate-possibilities conception of free will is philosophically incoherent regardless of whether consciousness is material, immaterial, or emergent.
The move isolates the skeptic's case from contested theories of mind and neuroscience, presenting conceptual incoherence as sufficient against libertarian freedom.
The audience suggestion that whether consciousness emerges from the brain may determine the viability of the debate's competing free-will positions.
O'Connor expresses uncertainty about materialism but says Libet-style experiments and mind theories are unnecessary because alternate possibility under identical conditions is incoherent.
A genuinely random event cannot itself have a cause, although quantum probability may be only a useful mathematical model rather than physical reality.
The distinction between randomness and causation bears on whether a causal regress can terminate without producing the control required for free will.
The earlier question asking what could cause the randomness and whether it resembles an Epicurean swerve.
O'Connor explains that caused randomness would not be random, questions realist readings of quantum probability, and remains uncertain between first-cause and alternative cosmological accounts.
External force can severely restrict available actions and thereby obstruct a person's exercise of rational judgment and free will.
This move specifies how the defended capacity for free will relates to coercion and constrained circumstances without claiming unlimited control over outcomes.
The audience question about whether social rules, family pressure, and the desire for acceptance limit genuinely free action.
Biddle distinguishes coexisting desires, choices, and social conditions, arguing that coercive force narrows actionable options and can prevent independent rational decision-making.
The fundamental volitional choice concerns whether and how fully to activate one's mind, not the unrestricted selection of any desired action or outcome.
This is the defender's core definition of free will and directly separates a capacity to regulate awareness from ultimate control over circumstances or content.
The audience concern that external constraints and competing desires may prevent people from acting as they otherwise wish.
Biddle says circumstances delimit possible decisions, while people generally retain degrees of control over mental engagement, ranging from full-context awareness to evasion or drift.
Dependence of consciousness on a functioning brain does not establish that consciousness is identical to the brain's chemical and electrical processes.
The argument answers a materialist challenge that would otherwise reduce deliberation and choice to wholly physical processes and undermine the defended volitional capacity.
The audience argument that minds require brains and therefore thoughts and decisions are merely products of brain activity.

Biddle uses the difference between living organization and remaining matter after death to argue that dependent phenomena may still be distinct, then applies that distinction to consciousness and brain.
Perceptual phenomena such as sound, music, and color are not identical to the external physical waves involved in producing those experiences.
The perceptual analogy supports his broader distinction between consciousness and neural matter, which is being used to resist the materialist objection to free will.
The objection comparing a distinction between consciousness and brain activity to a distinction between music and sound waves.
Biddle argues that waves exist externally while experienced sound, music, and color arise through an organism's perceptual processing, illustrating a form-object distinction.
Free will is not inferred by proof but recognized as self-evident once it is correctly understood as regulation of one's degree of conscious awareness.
The move supplies the defender's epistemic basis for affirming free will and explains why challenges aimed at unrestricted choice address the wrong conception.
The audience proposal that inductive reasoning may provide a stronger proof of free will than the phenomenon of evasion.
Biddle places free will beneath ordinary proof as a directly observable capacity, contrasting control over awareness with the impossible power to alter necessary facts at will.
Free will governs only the narrow, high-leverage activation of conscious attention, not every action or process occurring within a human being.
This qualification prevents the pro position from overclaiming universal volitional control and sharply identifies the limited domain in which its free-will thesis operates.
The audience participant's premise that all human action results from choices and that desires and fears are themselves choice-based.
Biddle distinguishes chosen conduct from reflexes, bodily functions, and unconscious neural events, locating control solely in whether the conscious mind is activated.
Even conscious conduct under coercion remains technically a choice between desire-governed alternatives, although ordinary language reasonably describes it as forced.
The move applies the skeptic's central claim that conscious choices are governed by desires even when alternatives exist, directly testing whether available choice establishes free will.
Biddle's distinction between chosen actions and reflexive or unconscious actions, together with the earlier treatment of coercive force.
O'Connor limits the discussion to conscious action, analyzes coercion as a technically available but desire-structured choice, and extends the point to family and social pressure.
In a coercive choice, activating free will enables a person to weigh competing values and desires correctly rather than merely follow the strongest unexamined impulse.
This closing move directly contrasts the pro account of rational volitional evaluation with the con claim that action is ultimately governed by whichever desire prevails.
O'Connor's claim that coerced and socially constrained conscious actions remain choices ultimately governed by the agent's desires.
Biddle agrees that bodily events may lack choice but argues that conscious mental activation can order values, compare survival with appearance, and produce the rational decision.
